name: Chlortalidone

card.summary: A long-acting thiazide-like blood-pressure diuretic; a possible water pill in forum lists, with no appearance data.
card.note: Prescription-only; can lower potassium and sodium and raise blood sugar.

quick.overview:
Chlortalidone (also spelled chlorthalidone) is a long-acting thiazide-like diuretic and a first-line treatment for high blood pressure. It has been in medical use since 1960.

It is included in this wiki as a diuretic sometimes grouped with water pills. No study has examined it for puffiness or any appearance goal.
quick.mechanism: It blocks the sodium-chloride symporter in the distal convoluted tubule and also inhibits carbonic anhydrase. Its half-life of about 40 hours is longer than that of hydrochlorothiazide.[1]
quick.risks: Reported effects include low potassium and sodium, high blood sugar, dizziness, erectile dysfunction, high uric acid and photosensitivity. It is prescription-only and banned in some sports.[1]

lead: Chlortalidone (chlorthalidone) is an oral thiazide-like diuretic used as a first-line treatment for hypertension and for edema from heart, liver or kidney disease. It is also used for nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, renal tubular acidosis and preventing calcium kidney stones.[1]

It was patented in 1957 and entered medical use in 1960, and it is on the WHO Essential Medicines List.[1][2] It is slowly absorbed and has a half-life of around 40 hours, which Wikipedia says may explain greater blood-pressure effect compared with hydrochlorothiazide.[1]
No published research has tested chlortalidone for facial depuffing or other cosmetic uses.

paras: Chlortalidone treats hypertension, edema, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, renal tubular acidosis and calcium oxalate stone recurrence. Wikipedia reports it reduces left ventricular mass and that evidence for Meniere disease is limited to small, low-quality studies.[1]

Wikipedia states a meta-analysis found greater blood-pressure reduction than hydrochlorothiazide with similar side effects, and that low doses worked about as well as higher ones in ALLHAT.[1] Reviews disagree on whether its risks match or exceed those of hydrochlorothiazide, with some reporting more hypokalaemia and hyponatraemia.[1]

Common effects include low potassium and sodium, high blood sugar, dizziness and erectile dysfunction; others include low magnesium, high calcium and uric acid, gout, photosensitivity and pancreatitis. It is considered a less preferred option in pregnancy.[1]

The drug is banned in some sports because diuretics aid weight-class cutting and can mask other substances. Wikipedia also notes an FDA recall of over 11,000 bottles of 25 mg tablets for failed dissolution specifications.[1] The sources reviewed contain no substantive discussion of chlortalidone in looksmaxxing communities.

No studies found on chlortalidone for facial depuffing or other appearance goals. Registered trials examine it in hypertension, including a 940-participant comparison of treatment regimens and combination trials with azilsartan.[3][4]
